newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Gunfire disrupts royalist rally in Albania.
newsitem.headline: Gunfire disrupts royalist rally in Albania.

text.p: Gunfire erupted during a march by Albanian monarchists on Thursday, reportedly killing one person and pitching central Tirana into confusion in the aftermath of an election which is set to catapult the Socialists into power.

But with counting still incomplete four days before a run-off round, the pan-European organisation overseeing the vote urged President Sali Berisha and all political parties against putting obstacles in the way of the electoral process.

Danish Foreign Minister Niels Helveg Petersen, current chairman of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), said the future of international aid to Albania depended on authorities giving their full cooperation.

The shooting melee occurred just after 1 p.m. outside the offices of the Central Election Commission and the public prosecutor was later quoted by the official ATA news agency as saying one person was killed and one injured.
Backers of self-proclaimed king Leka I were denouncing the results of a referendum held alongside the election in which voters appeared to oppose reinstating the monarchy.
Witnesses saw several people pointing pistols in the air as Leka strode through the crowd, dressed in fatigues and a grey beret. He was carrying two pistols of his own.

The first crack of gunfire sparked at least 10 minutes of shooting, which appeared to be mostly in the air. Marchers, bystanders and journalists scattered for cover and at least four hand grenades exploded. No one was hurt inside.
Monarchists said the police opened fire first. Police denied it.
The deputy head of the Election Commission, Fatos Klosi, said he was certain the monarchists were the first to shoot.
"I'm sure they were headed for the room where the commission was sitting. They knew where to go," he said.
Klosi said results had been tallied from all but seven of 115 districts, but he was unable to give a detailed breakdown.
Earlier results had given the Socialists and their allies 49 seats to eight for Berisha's Democrats. At least 25 races will go through to a run-off where no candidate won 50 percent.

In his warning to ensure the election proceeded properly, Petersen urged "President (Sali) Berisha and all parties involved to cease forthwith any attempt to put obstacles in the way of the electoral process".

The head of the OSCE Albania mission, former Austrian Chancellor Franz Vranitzky, had earlier complained in a statement of a lack of cooperation from electoral officials "seemingly due to political interference".
But the head of Albania's electoral commission, Kritaq Kume, denied that officials were absent or under pressure.
Security arrangements between the two rounds of the election were further complicated by the resignation of Interior Minister Belul Celo.

A statement from Berisha's office said Celo had stepped down for "personal reasons" and Socialist Prime Minister Bashkim Fino asked to propose a replacement. Under an agreement setting up Albania's interim government and holding the early election, the minister must be from Berisha's Democratic Party.
Uncertainty over whether Celo was still in his post sparked a row over control of the security forces between the president and prime minister on Wednesday.
The monarchists had marched from Skanderbeg Square down Tirana's main boulevard to converge on election headquarters, shouting slogans against Socialist leader Fatos Nano.
Berisha, who has acknowledged the Democrats' defeat pledged to step down when the new government takes power, called on all Albanians to remain calm.
Prime Minister Fino suggested the monarchists were being manipulated, but did not say who might be responsible.

The complicated nature of Albanian politics has been further muddied by the demands of royalists who want to bring back Leka, son of Zog, Albania's last king who fled into exile in 1939 after Italian Fascist forces invaded Albania.

Leka, who has spent most of his life in western Europe and South Africa, alleges that the referendum vote has been rigged against him. Partial results showed around 36 percent voted for Leka and 64 percent against.
